title: The stand at Chamkaur
hookLine: the Guru's elder sons, Ajit Singh and Jujhar Singh, die fighting at Chamkaur, aged about eighteen and fourteen

cards: After the river, the Guru's group was tiny. Tradition says about forty Sikhs, and his two elder sons, Ajit Singh, about eighteen, and Jujhar Singh, about fourteen.
They reached a village called Chamkaur, cold, wet and exhausted, and took shelter in a mud-walled house on high ground, more farmhouse than fort. By morning, the pursuing army had surrounded it.
Tradition speaks of a vast force against forty. There was no way out. Today, two young men who walked out through the gate.

teach.b: Inside the walls, the Sikhs decided to go out in small groups of five to hold the enemy back, knowing those who went would not come back. Tradition says the elder son, Ajit Singh, asked his father's permission to go.
The Guru gave it, helped arm him, and watched from the wall as his son fought and fell.
Then the younger one, Jujhar Singh, came to him. Tradition says the Guru asked if he was sure. He was.
His father sent him out too, and he fell like his brother. Both of the Guru's elder sons died at Chamkaur, on the same day. Then came something that shows what the Khalsa had become.

The Sikhs left inside urged the Guru to escape, so the community would not lose its Guru. He refused. So, tradition says, five of them, speaking as the Panj Pyare, as the Khalsa itself, gave him an order.

teach.h: THE FIVE ORDER THE GURU TO GO.
teach.b: And the Guru, who had knelt to receive amrit from five of his Sikhs, obeyed the five again. He slipped out in the night.
One Sikh, Bhai Sangat Singh, who resembled him, put on the Guru's plumed turban and stayed behind so the enemy would think he was still inside. The Sikhs who stayed died at Chamkaur.
Tradition says that among them was Kirpa Singh, the same man who, as Pandit Kirpa Ram, had come from Kashmir to ask Guru Tegh Bahadur for help. Two sons, and a handful of Sikhs, in a mud house.

how: Each December, Sikhs remember the battle of Chamkaur and the elder Sahibzade, Ajit Singh and Jujhar Singh, with gatherings at Gurdwara Katalgarh Sahib and Gurdwara Garhi Sahib in Chamkaur.

games.q: who's who at Chamkaur — tap the pairs.
p: wore the Guru's turban and stayed
once Pandit Kirpa Ram of Kashmir

s: the Guru chose to leave Chamkaur on his own
tradition says he refused, and five Sikhs, as the Khalsa, ordered him to go.
both elder sons died on the same day
Ajit Singh and Jujhar Singh both fell at Chamkaur.
the Sikhs went out in small groups of five
tradition says they went out a few at a time to hold the enemy back.

games.q: you're the Guru. your sons have fallen, and five of your Sikhs, speaking as the Khalsa, order you to escape. what do you do?
o: refuse and stay to the end.
obey the five and slip out at night.
games.why: the Guru obeyed the five, as he had knelt to them at Vaisakhi. Bhai Sangat Singh wore his turban and stayed behind.

practice: Sit quietly for the elder sons, and say the two names softly: Ajit Singh, about eighteen; Jujhar Singh, about fourteen.
Think of someone you know at those ages, and sit with the feeling respectfully, the way people sit at a memorial, without needing to do anything with it. If you pray, you can pray in your own words.

wordCard.voice: Chamkaur. The village where Guru Gobind Singh's elder sons, Ajit Singh and Jujhar Singh, died fighting, and the five ordered the Guru to live.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: Chamkaur, the village where the elder sons fell.

carryVoice: Your line: they stood. Two brothers, one day, and the same gate out. Day eighty-nine, done.
